intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. Each note explains a slide, tells you what to remember and warns you where people slip. Work the section exercises in pencil, check yourself against the recall questions, and write your own notes in the margins.

sections.title: What Is Data Literacy?
sections.big_idea: Data literacy is **judgement before statistics**: asking the right question of a number matters more than computing it.
in_plain_words: Development work runs on targets, indicators and surveys. Data literacy is the ability to find, read, question, interpret and communicate data, and to notice when it is misused. Technique can be looked up, while judgement stops a competent analysis from answering the wrong question.

Numbers climb a ladder from data to information to knowledge to decision, and error can enter at every step. **Numbers feel objective, yet each dataset embeds choices** about what to measure, which categories to use and whom to ask. Five habits keep you honest: where from, what measured, who missing, how sure, what decision.

diagram.caption: each step adds interpretation and can add error

key_terms.meaning: The capacity to read, question, interpret and communicate data.
The base a count is measured against.
How thoroughly a place was surveyed, which can mimic burden.
A measurable marker standing in for something we cannot observe.
Units that did not get the programme, used to judge change.

worked_example.title: Climb the ladder with care
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: 1,240 children are weighed and 18 per cent are underweight.
steps: Ask the denominator question: weighed, or eligible? A different base changes the 18%.
Knowledge: the 223 sit mostly in 3 hamlets. Ask whether those hamlets were visited more thoroughly.
Decision: feed those hamlets only if the concentration reflects need and not measurement effort.
worked_example.answer: About 223 children, but the decision waits on the denominator and on how evenly the hamlets were measured.

mistakes: Treating a number as neutral when its categories and respondents were chosen by someone.
Reading a before-and-after change as the programme's effect with no comparison group.
Using a state estimate for a block because it is the only number available.
Letting caveats drop out by the time a decision needs a single number.

recall.q: What are the five habits of a data-literate practitioner?
recall.a: Ask where it came from, what it measures, who is missing, how sure we are, and what decision it serves.

recall.q: What goes wrong at the Information step of the ladder?
recall.a: Which reference standard was used, and whether the denominator is those weighed or those eligible.

recall.q: What does the household-head example show?
recall.a: Asking one person about everyone gives that person's view, and the gap is systematically gendered.

recall.q: Why can a definition change matter?
recall.a: It can halve a rate overnight.

recall.q: Why does the deck say data literacy is judgement first?
recall.a: Technique can be looked up, while judgement stops a competent analysis answering the wrong question.

sections.title: Types & Sources of Data
sections.big_idea: Know the **type** of data, where it came from and **the level it was designed for** before you use it.
in_plain_words: Data comes as quantitative or qualitative, primary or secondary, structured or unstructured, and as cross-section, time series or panel. Each pairing has a question it can answer. Exhaust good secondary data before collecting your own, since re-collecting spends respondents' time they already gave once.

India's official system covers most needs: Census, NFHS, PLFS, SRS, HMIS. **A survey is only reliable down to the level it was designed for**, usually state or district. Administrative data and big data are useful but record only those who show up or who are connected.

diagram.caption: six ways to sort a dataset

key_terms.meaning: Data you collect yourself.
Data someone else collected.
The same units tracked over time.
Units lost between rounds, often non-randomly.
A by-product of delivering a scheme.
A number used to judge people drifts in the flattering direction.

worked_example.title: Why a block claim fails
worked_example.setup: NFHS-5 interviewed about 636,000 households across 707 districts.
steps: A district estimate of anaemia rests on roughly 900 households, and a block holds only a share of them.
A cell of 900 respondents at 62% is 900 × 62 ÷ 100 = 558 people.
A cell of nine at 62% is 9 × 62 ÷ 100 = 5.58 people, a percentage with almost no information.
worked_example.answer: About 900 households per district supports a district claim, and a block or tiny cell does not.

mistakes: Using a state-level survey estimate to make claims about a single block.
Treating a time series as proof that the same households improved.
Reading administrative data as if it described people who were never served.
Ignoring panel attrition when the hardest-to-find households drop out.

recall.q: Which dataset answers anaemia and child nutrition questions?
recall.a: NFHS.

recall.q: Which dataset gives monthly facility-level service delivery?
recall.a: HMIS.

recall.q: What is the rule of thumb for primary and secondary data?
recall.a: Exhaust good secondary data before collecting primary data.

recall.q: Why can a district poverty rate fall in a time series without anyone escaping poverty?
recall.a: Poor households may have migrated out.

recall.q: What test should you apply to any digital trace?
recall.a: Would the person you are most worried about appear in this dataset at all?

sections.title: From Concept to Indicator
sections.big_idea: Every indicator is **narrower than its concept**, and the gap is what a report must name.
in_plain_words: You cannot measure wellbeing directly. You break a concept into dimensions, pick an indicator for each, and collect data. Operationalisation fixes exactly what to count, for whom, over what period and in what units, and most arguments about numbers are really arguments about those choices.

The level of measurement decides which statistics are legal: nominal labels, ordinal ranks, interval gaps, ratio zero. A good indicator is valid, reliable, sensitive and feasible, and **reliability without validity is only consistent error**. Proxies and composite indices such as the MPI bundle choices that deserve naming.

diagram.caption: levels of measurement: more power as you go up

key_terms.meaning: The rule turning a concept into a measurement.
Measures what it claims to measure.
Gives the same answer on repeat measurement.
A measure that stands in for something hard to measure.
Several indicators bundled into one score.
How many are poor, times how deeply poor.

worked_example.title: Build a small MPI and test the cut-off
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: 20 per cent of households are poor and the poor are deprived at an average intensity of 40 per cent.
steps: The rule: poor means deprived in a weighted third or more.
A weighted third is 100 ÷ 3 = 33.3 per cent of the weights.
Move the cut-off and the headcount changes with no change on the ground.
worked_example.answer: The illustrative MPI is 0.08, and the headline depends on the chosen cut-off.

mistakes: Averaging district codes or treating a wealth quintile as a rupee amount.
Mistaking a stable series for a valid one.
Forgetting that proxies leak in a systematic direction.
Publishing an index score without its components.

recall.q: What four properties make an indicator trustworthy?
recall.a: Valid, reliable, sensitive and feasible.

recall.q: Which level of measurement allows ratios?
recall.a: Ratio, because it has equal gaps and a true zero.

recall.q: What is the problem with a mean wealth quintile of 3.2?
recall.a: The quintile is ordinal, so the gaps are not equal.

recall.q: Name two things an index hides.
recall.a: A bad component masked by a good score, and the weights that are value judgements.

recall.q: What does the MPI count as poor?
recall.a: A household deprived in a weighted third or more of its 12 indicators.

sections.title: Describing Data
sections.big_idea: Describe the **centre, the spread and the shape** of every variable before any analysis, and always ask 'out of how many?'.
in_plain_words: Before modelling, report N, missingness, centre and spread, shape and extremes. Use the median for money and land because a few large values drag the mean. Report a spread beside any centre, since two districts with one mean can be nothing alike.

Percentiles and quintiles are relative to a survey's own population. The normal curve helps only for roughly symmetric data, and most development data is skewed. **Never silently drop an outlier**: it may be an error or the whole story. Counts without a denominator mislead, so insist on rates.

children.label: Shape and extremes
items: Skew decides if the mean is honest

key_terms.meaning: The middle value when sorted.
Interquartile range, the middle 50 per cent.
A long tail of large values.
One of five equal-size groups.
The base that turns a count into a rate.
A number like 99 used to mean missing or refused.

worked_example.title: Same count, different rate
worked_example.setup: A report says '500 dropouts'. Compare two possible bases.
steps: Same count, a crisis in one case and a small figure in the other.
'Cases doubled' means 3 to 6 in one place and 3,000 to 6,000 in another.
worked_example.answer: The base decides the meaning: 83.3% against 0.83% for the same 500.

mistakes: Reporting a mean income for a skewed variable.
Deleting the one block with triple the dropout without investigating it.
Comparing the poorest quintile across states as if it were one living standard.
Colouring a map by raw counts, which usually shows population.

recall.q: Which average suits household income?
recall.a: The median, because income is right-skewed.

recall.q: What does the 68-95-99.7 rule claim?
recall.a: About 68 per cent of values lie within 1 SD, 95 per cent within 2 and 99.7 per cent within 3 in roughly normal data.

recall.q: Why can quintiles hide absolute change?
recall.a: The bottom fifth is always a fifth, so the share can stay put while the country grows richer.

recall.q: What is wrong with an age of 999?
recall.a: It is likely an undeclared missing code that would enter every average.

recall.q: What is the single highest-yield question?
recall.a: Out of how many?

sections.title: Visualising Data
sections.big_idea: A chart is an **argument you can see**, so state the finding first and keep the baseline honest.
in_plain_words: Pick the chart for the question: lines for time, bars for categories, scatter plots for relationships, histograms for distributions and choropleths for geography. Every honest chart carries a title that states the finding, labelled axes, a source and date, and a note on the denominator.

The most common lie is the truncated axis, which can make a 4-point rise look like a tripling. Strip chartjunk, use colour with intent and test in greyscale. **Split crowded charts into small multiples with a shared scale.** Sometimes a table beats a chart.

key_terms.meaning: A y-axis that does not start at zero.
Decoration that competes with the data.
Tufte's idea: maximise the ink that carries data.
Repeated small charts sharing a scale.
One hue from light to dark for ordered data.
A map coloured by a value per area.

worked_example.title: What a truncated axis does
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: two values of 92 and 96 are drawn on an axis that starts at 90.
steps: The taller bar looks 6 ÷ 2 = 3 times as tall, a tripling.
The true ratio: 96 ÷ 92 = 1.04, a rise of about 4 per cent.
worked_example.answer: The chart suggests a tripling, but the series rose about 4 per cent.

mistakes: Using a pie for change over time or 3-D anything.
Relying on red against green to separate categories.
Putting the source in the paragraph below the chart and leaving it off the chart.
Truncating an axis silently.

recall.q: Which chart suits change over time?
recall.a: A line chart.

recall.q: What five things does an honest chart need?
recall.a: A title stating the takeaway, labelled axes with units, an honest baseline, a source and date, and a note on denominator and exclusions.

recall.q: Why use direct labels?
recall.a: They remove the lookup step where readers give up.

recall.q: About what share of men have colour-vision deficiency?
recall.a: About 8 per cent.

recall.q: When does a table beat a chart?
recall.a: When exact values matter and people will look up or quote them.

sections.title: Relationships & Correlation
sections.big_idea: A correlation is a clue, and **five different explanations** can produce it.
in_plain_words: Correlation r runs from −1 to +1 and measures how closely points follow a line, and says nothing of how steep the line is. A near-zero r can hide a strong U-shape. Plot the data first, as Anscombe's four identical-statistic datasets show.

A pattern can come from A causing B, B causing A, a confounder, selection or chance. Group patterns do not transfer to individuals, a trend can reverse when you split the data, and extreme results drift back to average. **Say the other four explanations aloud before accepting a causal reading.**

key_terms.meaning: A third variable that drives both.
Inferring individual truths from group patterns.
A trend that reverses when subgroups are split.
Extreme values drift back toward average.
Four datasets with identical statistics and different shapes.
A pattern that arises from noise or shared trends.

worked_example.title: Simpson's paradox in two hospitals
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: Hospital A treats 20 mild and 80 severe patients; Hospital B treats 80 mild and 20 severe.
steps: A is better in both groups.
Overall survivors: A has 20 + 48 = 68 of 100 and B has 76 + 11 = 87 of 100.
worked_example.answer: A beats B within each group yet looks worse overall because it takes the severe cases.

mistakes: Reading r near zero as no relationship.
Quoting a time-series correlation where both series just trend upward.
Crediting a programme for gains that regression to the mean would produce.
Controlling for 'household characteristics' and assuming motivation is covered.

recall.q: What is Anscombe's lesson?
recall.a: Always plot the data, since identical summary statistics can hide different shapes.

recall.q: What is the ecological fallacy?
recall.a: Wrongly inferring something about individuals from a pattern seen only at group level.

recall.q: Why do programme areas sometimes look worse than others?
recall.a: Programmes are placed where need is greatest, which is reverse causation.

recall.q: What is the cure for regression to the mean in evaluation?
recall.a: A comparison group selected the same way.

recall.q: How do you remove most spurious time-series correlations?
recall.a: Look at year-on-year changes and leave the levels aside.

sections.title: Sampling & Surveys
sections.big_idea: Sampling works through **representativeness and absolute sample size**, and size can never repair bias.
in_plain_words: Define the population first, then the frame you can actually draw from, then the sample, then who really answers. Each gap lets bias in, and the frame is often the weakest link. Probability methods let chance choose and so allow a margin of error. Non-probability methods suit depth and hidden groups.

For a large population, accuracy depends on the absolute sample, with about 1,067 giving ±3 per cent. Halving the error needs roughly four times as many. **Bias does not shrink as the sample grows.** Weights restore the right population, and question wording is itself measurement.

nodes.label: Target population
nodes.sub: whom you want to learn about

nodes.label: Sampling frame
nodes.sub: the list you can draw from

diagram.caption: every gap is a place for bias to enter

key_terms.meaning: The list from which the sample is drawn.
Split into groups, then sample each.
Sample whole groups such as villages.
Extra variance from clustering.
The number of real people a respondent represents.
Answering how one thinks one should.

worked_example.title: Size and fraction
worked_example.setup: Use the deck's figures for ±3 per cent at 95 per cent confidence.
steps: The sample barely changed while the fraction fell a hundred-fold.
Halving the error to ±1.5 per cent needs about 4,000, which is 4,000 ÷ 1,067 = 3.75 times the sample.
worked_example.answer: About 1,000 to 1,070 respondents give ±3% for any large population; halving the error needs about 3.75 times as many.

mistakes: Describing the sample as 'a random sample of households' without naming the frame.
Attaching a margin of error to a non-probability sample.
Analysing NFHS or PLFS unit data without the survey weights.
Arguing about sample size when the design is biased.

recall.q: Which sampling methods are probability methods?
recall.a: Simple random, systematic, stratified, cluster and multistage.

recall.q: What is the catch about a national sample of 1,000?
recall.a: It supports almost nothing about a district within it, because the district cell is tiny.

recall.q: Name three biases that size cannot fix.
recall.a: Selection, non-response and social-desirability bias.

recall.q: Why must you pilot a questionnaire?
recall.a: Clarifying questions reveal ambiguity and instant approved answers reveal leading items.

recall.q: Why stratify at design time?
recall.a: If a subgroup must be reported separately, filtering afterwards cannot recover it.

sections.title: Data Quality & Cleaning
sections.big_idea: Cleaning is the work itself, and a **repeatable, logged pipeline** is what lets you defend a number.
in_plain_words: Most of a data project is preparing data. The common faults are missing values, duplicates, inconsistent codes, impossible values, format drift and typos in keys. Most are preventable at collection with dropdowns, range checks and a required ID format.

The reason a value is missing matters more than how many are. Clean in a script, never edit the raw file, and log counts before and after every filter. **If you cannot redo it, you cannot trust it.** Document variables in a codebook and keep dated, named versions.

key_terms.meaning: Gaps unrelated to the value, the least harmful.
Gaps tied to the answer itself, such as refused income.
A script from raw data to result that anyone can rerun.
A data dictionary of variables, units and codes.
A rule that a value must lie within possible limits.
Data about your data.

worked_example.title: Log the drops
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a cleaning script starts with 4,200 records and ends with 3,180.
worked_example.answer: 1,020 records, 24.3% of the start, and the log shows why each was dropped.

mistakes: Editing the raw file by hand in a spreadsheet.
Dropping every row with a gap and deleting the people you care about.
Leaving 99 or 999 undeclared so it enters averages.
Writing the codebook at the end from memory.

recall.q: What is the golden rule of cleaning?
recall.a: Never edit the raw file.

recall.q: Which dirty-data problem inflates counts silently?
recall.a: Duplicates.

recall.q: What should you compare at every merge?
recall.a: Unique-ID counts against record counts.

recall.q: What is the most valuable validation step?
recall.a: Reviewing the first days of fieldwork data.

recall.q: What does the metadata document hold?
recall.a: What each variable means, codes, how and when collected, limitations and who to ask.

sections.title: Reading Data Critically
sections.big_idea: Eight questions catch most bad statistics, starting with **uncertainty, base rates and the framing of change**.
in_plain_words: Every estimate is a range, and overlapping intervals often mean no real difference. Statistical significance is a narrow claim about chance and says nothing about size, so ask for the effect size. Even an accurate test for a rare condition produces mostly false positives.

Percent and percentage points differ, and relative change without the absolute counts is built to impress. Cherry-picked baselines and the garden of forking paths produce false findings with no cheating. **Write the analysis plan before you look at the data.**

key_terms.meaning: The range around an estimate.
Unlikely under the null, silent on size.
How common the thing is to begin with.
The unit for a difference between two percentages.
Choosing baseline, indicator or subgroup to flatter.
Reporting only the slice that looks significant.

worked_example.title: The base-rate trap
worked_example.setup: A test is 99 per cent accurate for a condition affecting 1 in 1,000. Test 100,000 people.
worked_example.answer: About 9%, roughly 1 in 11, so most positives are false.

mistakes: Ranking districts when their confidence intervals overlap.
Reading 'significant' as large or important.
Quoting '25 per cent more' without the absolute counts.
Reporting the one surprising subgroup result.

recall.q: What is the difference between a 25 per cent rise and a 5 percentage-point rise?
recall.a: They can describe the same change from 20 to 25 per cent; one is relative and one is absolute.

recall.q: What does the base-rate trap show?
recall.a: A 99 per cent accurate test for a rare condition yields mostly false positives.

recall.q: What does statistical significance not tell you?
recall.a: How large or important the effect is.

recall.q: How do you guard against forking paths?
recall.a: Write the analysis plan and name the primary outcome and subgroups first.

recall.q: Name two questions from the reader's checklist.
recall.a: Out of how many, and who is missing from the count.

sections.title: Data Ethics, Privacy & Equity
sections.big_idea: Every data point is a person, and **consent, privacy and who is counted** are part of the method.
in_plain_words: Rows are people, often poor and without power over their information. Consent is real only when the person understands, can decline at no cost and knows how to withdraw. Anonymisation takes more than deleting names, because village plus age plus caste plus occupation can identify one person.

The DPDP Act, 2023 covers anyone handling personal digital data, including NGOs. Disaggregation shows who an average hides, and some people are systematically uncounted. **What is not counted is not funded.** Give findings back to the community in usable form.

diagram.root: Protecting the people in the data

children.label: Consent
items: Know what, why and for how long

children.label: Power
items: Share a copy of the data

diagram.caption: four duties to the people behind the rows

key_terms.meaning: Knowing what is collected, why and how it is used, and freely agreeing.
A trait that can identify a person in combination.
Hiding counts too small to be safe.
India's 2023 data-protection law.
Splitting results by group.
Value flowing to outsiders while respondents see nothing back.

worked_example.title: Disaggregate an average
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a programme has 1,000 beneficiaries, 900 from one group and 100 from an excluded group.
worked_example.answer: The headline reads 73% while one group is reached at 10%.

mistakes: Counting a signature on an unexplained form as consent.
Calling a dataset anonymised because names were removed.
Assuming a small NGO is exempt from the DPDP Act.
Treating missing groups as random gaps.

recall.q: When is consent real?
recall.a: When the person knows what is collected and why, declining costs nothing, a purpose and period are named, and withdrawal is explained.

recall.q: What is a quasi-identifier?
recall.a: A combination such as age, place and caste that can re-identify a person.

recall.q: From when do the DPDP Act duties apply?
Name two groups that are systematically under-counted.
recall.a: Seasonal migrants and homeless people, among others in the deck.

recall.q: What are two cheap corrections to data colonialism?
recall.a: A return visit to share results in the local language, and a copy of the data collected.

sections.title: Tools & Further Reading
sections.big_idea: Habits matter more than tools, and **the methodology note comes before the data**.
in_plain_words: Start with spreadsheets and learn pivot tables. Move to R or Python when the analysis will be repeated or must be reproducible, use Stata or SPSS where collaborators do, and use QGIS for anything spatial. A documented spreadsheet beats an undocumented script.

Open sources include data.gov.in, the Census, NFHS, MoSPI and the UDISE+ and HMIS portals. **Save every file with its download date**, because portals revise. Reading the methodology note teaches you the sample design, definitions and lowest valid level before you quote a figure.

key_terms.meaning: Free mobile survey collection tools.
Free, open-source GIS.
Document giving design, definitions and valid levels.
The version or date of a dataset.
India's open government data portal.

worked_example.title: Pick the tool
worked_example.setup: Match each task to a tool using the deck's rule of when each is worth it.
steps: A one-off summary of 40 rows shared with a programme officer: spreadsheet.
A quarterly analysis that must reproduce each time: R or Python.
A partner who already works in Stata: Stata or SPSS.
A map of block-level coverage: QGIS.
worked_example.answer: Spreadsheet, R or Python, Stata or SPSS, and QGIS in that order.

mistakes: Choosing a tool before the thinking is clear.
Using a portal file without recording its download date.
Skipping the methodology note.
Reading the whole reading list instead of the free NFHS and PLFS notes first.

recall.q: When is a spreadsheet worth it?
recall.a: When the work is small, one-off and shared with non-analysts.

recall.q: What does the methodology note contain?
recall.a: The sample design, the definitions and the lowest level at which estimates hold.

recall.q: Which tool suits mobile survey collection?
recall.a: KoboToolbox or ODK.

recall.q: Why record a download date?
recall.a: Portals update and revise, and a vintage cannot be reproduced without it.

recall.q: What is the deck's most useful free reading?
recall.a: The NFHS and PLFS survey methodology notes.

notes.2: Eleven sections run in a deliberate order: what data is, where it comes from, what it stands for, then how to describe, draw and relate it, how it was collected and cleaned, how to read it, and how to treat the people in it. Keep that order in mind as you go.
notes.4: The right-hand column of the table is the course in miniature. Each row pairs a technique with the **judgement** that tells you when it applies. You can look up a formula in a minute. Noticing that an average is the wrong summary stops a competent analysis from answering the wrong question.
notes.5: Read down the second column of the table. Every decision you make this quarter rests on a data question you probably never labelled as one: reliability at block level, compared with what, the earlier trend, out of how many. The warning sits on row two, where **before and after with no comparison group** inflates claims.
notes.6: Walk up the ladder one step at a time and ask what can go wrong at each. The children example turns 1,240 weighed into a feeding decision. The trap sits at the top: if three hamlets were visited more thoroughly, they show more of everything, so **measurement effort can pass for measured burden**.
notes.7: Learn the five habits as questions you can ask aloud: where from, what measured, who is missing, how sure, what decision. They need no statistics, which makes them easy to ask in a meeting. The fifth is the most underrated. If **no plausible value would change a decision**, the number is decoration.
notes.8: Numbers carry choices someone made earlier: what to measure, which categories, whom to ask, what counts as a case, what unit to report. None shows in the spreadsheet. Take the third row: asking the household head about everyone gives **the head's view**, and the gap is systematically gendered.
notes.9: Use this slide to plan your study. Each section row says what you will be able to do afterwards. The one-hour route is named at the bottom: section 6, section 9 and slide 38 on denominators. The examples are Indian, so knowing which dataset answers which question is part of the skill.
notes.11: Pair the two families by question. How many and did it fall are quantitative. Why and what did families think are qualitative. The alternating table is the argument: a serious programme question needs both in sequence. Watch for qualitative work as decoration, such as **three quotes picked to illustrate a finding already decided**.
notes.12: Use this rule of thumb: **exhaust good secondary data before collecting primary data**. The table shows the trade. Primary gives you control at high cost, while secondary is cheap but may not fit your question. The ethical point is easy to miss, because re-collecting what exists spends respondents' time they already gave once.
notes.13: Sort your own files into the three types. Most M&E sits in structured tables, while call logs, photographs and field notes pile up unused. The third row of the table marks where **unused evidence** sits. A cheap first step is to code one quarter of helpline text against a short list of categories.
notes.14: Match the data form to the question. A cross-section shows how things stand now, a time series shows whether the aggregate moved, and a panel follows the same units. Remember two traps: a district rate can fall because **poor households left**, and panel attrition can flatter results by losing those who did worst.
notes.15: Learn the six sources by name and by question. NFHS covers anaemia and child nutrition, PLFS covers work, the Census covers population by village, SRS covers infant mortality and HMIS covers monthly service delivery. Each holds only down to a certain level, and **the next slide explains which**.
notes.16: Hold this rule: the Census counts everyone and surveys infer from a sample. A survey is reliable only down to the level it was designed for, usually state or district. An NFHS figure for a block is **a claim the sample never supported**. Use the state figure as labelled context instead.
notes.17: These sizes show what the surveys can and cannot do. Size buys district-level precision and comparison across rounds. It buys neither block estimates nor every cross-tabulation. Always check the unweighted count behind a percentage, since 62 per cent of nine respondents says far less than 62 per cent of 900.
notes.18: Administrative data is what your programme already generates, so it is cheap and continuous. Its defining limit is in the first row: it records **who was served**, and the excluded are absent by construction. Watch the incentive on each field, since a number used to judge the person entering it drifts upward.
notes.19: Treat digital traces as a supplement. Mobile records, night-lights and transaction logs help where surveys are slow, but each leaves out a group. Use the test at the foot of the slide: **would the person you worry about most appear in this dataset at all?** If they would not, the data cannot speak for them.
notes.21: Measurement is a bridge from concept to indicator. Follow the chain: women's empowerment, then dimensions, then an indicator such as visiting a health centre alone, then survey data. The third column is what vanishes from reports. Once a number exists, people **drop the words 'proxy for'** and use the concept's name.
notes.22: Operationalisation is the exact rule behind a number: what to count, for whom, over what period, in what units and counted by whom. Most disagreements about numbers are disagreements about these. Write the definition in one sentence per indicator **before collection**. A year later it is the document everyone asks for.
notes.23: Memorise the four levels as a ladder: nominal labels, ordinal order, interval equal gaps, ratio true zero. The level decides which statistics are valid, and software will not warn you. A wealth quintile is a rank, so a mean of 3.2 is questionable. The Likert case is **disputed**, and a median costs nothing.
notes.24: Four tests for a trustworthy indicator: valid, reliable, sensitive, feasible. Use them as a checklist when you choose between two candidates. An indicator can pass three and fail the fourth, so **ask about feasibility early**, before you fall for one that nobody can afford to collect.
notes.25: Reliable means consistent and valid means correct. A scale that reads 2 kg high every time is reliable and wrong. You can have reliability without validity but never the reverse. The fourth row matters most: asking men about women's decision-making is **consistently the wrong respondent**, and a stable series looks trustworthy because it does not move.
notes.26: A proxy measures A to learn about B, and every proxy leaks. Use the table to name what each one misses: assets miss debt, night-lights miss the informal economy, enrolment misses attendance. Put the gap in one sentence in your report, such as **'we measure enrolment, which is not attendance'**.
notes.27: An index buys attention and spends detail. Use the four questions on any index: who chose the weights, can a bad component hide, is the cut-off a choice, are components correlated. Always publish the components with the score, because **the index is for attention and the components are for decisions**.
notes.28: The MPI is headcount times intensity, built from 12 indicators in three dimensions. A household is poor if deprived in a weighted third or more, so changing the threshold changes the rate **with no change on the ground**. Read its methodology note to see a poverty rate as a definition applied to data.
notes.30: Describe before you model. Ask what is typical, how much values vary and what shape they take. The table lists what to report first: N, missingness, centre and spread, shape and extremes. Plot every variable once, because **five minutes of histograms** catch a spike at zero or a wall at 99 that no summary shows.
notes.31: Choose the summary by the variable. Use the median for money and land, the mean for roughly symmetric things like child height, the mode for categories. When you must give a mean on skewed data, **report the median beside it**. The gap between them shows how concentrated the top of the distribution is.
notes.32: Look at the chart: one rich household pulls the mean to ₹31k while the typical household sits at ₹12k. Reporting the mean describes **a village that does not exist**. The data are illustrative, but the pattern is real for income and land. Make it a reflex to compare mean and median.
notes.33: Never report an average alone. Range is defined by outliers, IQR holds up for skewed data, standard deviation suits roughly symmetric data and the p90/p10 ratio compares inequality across places. Two districts with the same mean can be **an equal place and a polarised one**, and only spread tells you which.
notes.34: Quintiles divide a population into five equal-count groups, ranked by assets in NFHS. Remember they are **relative to that survey's population**, so the poorest quintile in Kerala and in Bihar are different living standards. They also cannot show absolute change, since the bottom fifth is always a fifth.
notes.35: Look at the two shapes: a symmetric curve beside a right-skewed one with a long tail. Income, landholding and firm size are almost always right-skewed. That is the moment to distrust the mean and reach for the median. The chart is illustrative, so use it to **train your eye on the tail**.
notes.36: The 68, 95 and 99.7 per cent figures apply only to roughly normal data such as height or measurement error. Most development data sits in the right column of the table, with a floor at zero and a long tail. Check with a histogram. Sample means still tend towards normal, so **confidence intervals work on skewed variables**.
notes.37: An outlier is a question, and the answer decides the action. A household of 80 may be a hostel or a typing slip. A block with triple the dropout may be the finding. Watch for codes like 99 and 999 left undeclared, because they **enter every average silently**. Flag, investigate and say what you did.
notes.38: Ask 'out of how many?' of every count. 500 dropouts means different things out of 600 and out of 60,000, and cases doubling from 3 to 6 differs from 3,000 to 6,000. The map version matters most: **a map coloured by raw counts is usually a population map**. Use rates on choropleths.
notes.40: A chart is an argument, so decide what it should show before you open software. The table lists when a chart works and when it fails: the reader sees the intended comparison, visual size matches the numbers, axes are labelled, and it survives black and white. **Say the sentence first**, then put it in the title.
notes.41: Use this table as a lookup. Time calls for lines, categories for bars, shares for stacked bars, relationships for scatter plots, distributions for histograms and geography for choropleths. The right-hand column names the traps: pies for change over time, 3-D anything, and **maps coloured by raw counts**.
notes.42: Every honest chart carries five things: a title that states the finding, labelled axes with units, an honest baseline, a source and date, and a note on denominator and exclusions. The fourth row matters because **percentages of nine cases look like percentages**. Put the source on the chart, since charts travel without their paragraph.
notes.43: Compare the two panels. The same data, with the axis starting at 90, makes a 4-point rise look like a tripling. Truncation is the most common way charts lie. Check **where every bar chart starts**, and see the checklist slide for the one case where truncation is justified if it is labelled.
notes.44: Tufte's rule is to maximise the data-ink ratio. Strip 3-D effects, heavy gridlines, decoration and rainbow palettes, and keep direct labels, annotation, source, units and N. The fastest single improvement is to **replace a legend with direct labels**, because the lookup step is where readers give up.
notes.45: Use colour to carry meaning: sequential for ordered data, a single accent for the point, and consistent meaning across charts. About 8 per cent of men have colour-vision deficiency, so red against green alone fails them. Test by **printing in greyscale**. If the categories still separate, the chart survives.
notes.46: When a chart gets crowded, split it. Small multiples repeat a small identical chart so the eye compares shapes, and the **shared scale** on every panel makes the comparison honest. Dual-axis charts deserve their reputation, since two scales can be made to cross wherever the designer wishes.
notes.47: Match the format to the reader. Use a table for exact values people will look up or quote, and a chart for pattern. Six numbers in a table are read accurately. Sort by the column that matters, because **alphabetical order hides every pattern** the table contains.
notes.48: Run the six questions before you publish, then use the five-row table as the fail states. Memorise the last check: **would someone who disagrees find it fair?** Most misleading charts come from people arguing for something true. Truncating an axis can be right for a narrow band, and the rule is to never do it silently.
notes.50: The coefficient r runs from −1 to +1, and the table says what each value does and does not mean. Remember row two: an r near zero can hide a **strong U-shaped relationship**. Strength also differs from effect size. Plot the data before you conclude anything from the coefficient.
notes.51: The scatter shows states with higher female literacy tending to have lower fertility. Read it as a negative correlation, then pause. The slide asks **does literacy cause lower fertility?** and the next slides give you reasons to hold back. The chart is illustrative, patterned on Census 2011 and NFHS-5.
notes.52: Learn the five explanations for a correlation: A causes B, B causes A, C causes both, selection and chance. Programme areas that look worse than others usually show **reverse causation**, since programmes go where need is greatest. Before accepting a causal reading, say the other four aloud and explain why each is unlikely.
notes.53: A confounder drives both variables. Heat explains ice cream and drowning, and wealth explains toilets and child height. Confounding is **the default state of observational data**. Controlling for 'household characteristics' covers only what was measured, and motivation, information and connections are usually missing from the dataset.
notes.54: Spurious patterns come from many comparisons, from two series that both trend over time, from small samples and from selective write-ups. The guards in the table are to state the number of comparisons, compare changes and not levels, report N, and pre-specify what you test. **Differencing removes most time-trend correlations**.
notes.55: Anscombe's four datasets share means, variances, correlation (r = 0.82) and a regression line, yet look nothing alike: a line, a curve, a line with one outlier and a vertical cluster with one distant point. The instruction is short: **plot it** before you quote any correlation or fit any line.
notes.56: Group patterns do not transfer to individuals. States with higher female literacy have lower fertility, which says nothing about any particular literate woman. This fallacy is common because **group data is what gets published**. The reverse error, assuming a group acts like its typical member, also exists.
notes.57: A trend can reverse when you split the data. Hospital A can look worse overall because it takes the severe cases. Neither the aggregate nor the split is wrong, and which one answers your question depends on the decision. Make it a habit to look at **every aggregate broken down by the obvious grouping**.
notes.58: When you pick the worst performers and re-measure, they usually improve with no intervention, because extremes contain luck that does not repeat. This is regression to the mean, and it **inflates before-and-after comparisons** of targeted programmes. The cure is a comparison group selected the same way.
notes.60: A sample works because of representativeness more than size. Sampling buys speed, depth and repeatability at the cost of uncertainty and small-area detail. The second row is the real trade-off: programme staff want block numbers, surveys are designed for state or district, and **wanting a number does not create the precision**.
notes.61: Follow the four steps from target population through frame and sample to respondents. Each gap is a place where bias enters. The weakest link is usually the frame: a list of phone owners is not a list of citizens. **Always report the frame**, which tells the reader who could never have been selected.
notes.62: Probability methods let chance choose, which is what allows a margin of error. Pick by situation: simple random with a full list, stratified when you need subgroup estimates, cluster when travel cost dominates, multistage for national surveys. **Stratify by what you will report on**, because filtering afterwards cannot recover it.
notes.63: Non-probability methods are legitimate for depth and hard-to-reach groups: convenience for piloting, purposive for information-rich cases, snowball for hidden populations, quota for fast polling. They answer 'what exists' and 'how does this work'. They cannot answer 'how many', so **never attach a margin of error** to them.
notes.64: Read the curve for its shape. About 1,067 respondents give ±3 per cent, but halving the error to ±1.5 per cent needs around 4,000. **Precision gets expensive fast**, so decide how much precision your decision really needs before you ask for a bigger sample.
notes.65: The surprise is that accuracy depends on the absolute sample and not on the share sampled. About 1,070 serve a million people and a national population alike. The catch is subgroups: a sample that supports a national figure supports little about a district within it. **Plan sample size for each estimate** you will report.
notes.66: Size fixes noise and never bias. The biases to know are selection, non-response, survivorship and social desirability, with coverage, enumerator selection and recall in the table. A bigger biased sample is a more confident wrong answer. Watch enumerator selection: **without a fixed rule, interviewers complete the easy households**.
notes.67: Weights make each respondent stand for the right number of real people, correcting for unequal selection, deliberate over-sampling and non-response. Using NFHS or PLFS unit data **without weights gives wrong totals**. Use the weight variable named in the documentation and report unweighted counts beside weighted percentages.
notes.68: Question wording is measurement. Avoid leading questions, double-barrelled ones, long recall periods, undefined terms and questions that invite the socially approved reply. **Pilot every instrument** with about twenty people. Where they ask for clarification the item is ambiguous, and an instant approved answer signals a leading item.
notes.70: Plan for cleaning. Analysts spend most of a project preparing data, and the table's proportions are folklore and not a measured statistic. Cleaning is also where findings appear, such as duplicate households or a block with no March records. **Never budget two days of cleaning** for a fortnight of analysis.
notes.71: Learn the six dirty-data patterns: missing values, duplicates, inconsistent codes, impossible values, format drift and typos in keys. Most are preventable at collection with dropdowns, range checks and a required ID format. **Duplicates are the dangerous one**, because they inflate counts silently, so compare unique IDs with record counts at every merge.
notes.72: Before you delete or fill a gap, ask why it is missing. A skipped page does little harm, while the richest refusing to state income biases results. Dropping rows with gaps can delete the people you care about. Report the **percent missing for each variable**, every time; it takes two lines of code.
notes.73: Memorise the five steps: inspect, validate, fix, document, freeze. The golden rule is **never edit the raw file**, and every change lives in a script. Log counts before and after each filter. 'We started with 4,200 records and analysed 3,180' invites a question, and the log is your answer.
notes.74: Run the four tests: could a colleague rerun it, could you in six months, does the report match the script, is the data version recorded. Reproducibility lets a finding **survive the analyst leaving**. The minimum version needs no new tools: raw data, one script, one output and a short README with the source file and date.
notes.75: Build checks into the instrument: range checks, controlled lists, skip logic, unique-ID constraints and a daily review of the first week's data. The last row is worth more than the rest, because **a systematic misunderstanding found early can still be corrected**, while one found at analysis costs the whole variable.
notes.76: Metadata is data about your data. Write the data dictionary while collecting, covering what each variable means, its units, category and missing codes, how and when it was collected, known limits and who to ask. Documentation written at the end is **reconstructed from memory** and wrong where it matters.
notes.77: Keep the trail. Save raw extracts read-only and dated, name files with versions and dates, record the source and download date, and keep the cleaning script with the data. A dated folder and a text change log capture most of the benefit on day one, before you learn full **version control**.
notes.79: Every estimate is a range. The confidence interval is the honest version, and a decimal place makes a figure look exact. Before saying one district is worse than another, **check whether the intervals overlap**. A move from 51.8 to 52.1 per cent could be no change at all. The table shows how to read each case.
notes.80: Statistical significance means a result is unlikely under a specific null hypothesis, and it says nothing about size or importance. With a big sample, trivial differences become significant. Always ask for the effect size: 'three percentage points higher, significantly' is a claim you can **weigh against the cost of acting**.
notes.81: Work the table through: 100,000 people, 100 with the condition, a 99 per cent accurate test. That gives about 99 true positives and 999 false positives, so a positive result means roughly 1 in 11. **Ask how common the thing is to begin with** whenever you read 'X per cent accurate'.
notes.82: A rise from 40 to 50 per cent is 10 percentage points and 25 per cent in relative terms. A press release chooses between them for effect. Write both once: **'from 20% to 25%, a rise of 5 percentage points (25% relative)'**. It removes the ambiguity at the cost of one clause.
notes.83: Relative change can hide tiny numbers. 'Cases doubled' from 2 to 4 is a doubling of almost nothing, and 'risk doubled' can mean 1 in 100,000 to 2 in 100,000. Pair the relative figure with the counts. The trick also runs in reverse, so **ask for both numbers in every direction**.
notes.84: Cherry-picking rarely uses a false number. The selection is the argument: a convenient start year, one indicator that improved, an unusual reference period, one favoured subgroup. Ask why this start, this indicator and this comparison. A baseline chosen as a **drought year** makes any later year look like recovery.
notes.85: If you slice the data twenty ways, about one slice will look significant by chance. Nobody needs to cheat for this: honest choices of outcome, subgroup, controls and cut-offs multiply the paths. The guard is an **analysis plan written before you see the data**, so later exploration is labelled as exploration.
notes.86: Keep the eight questions in your notebook and use them in meetings. They need no statistics: who produced it, how measured and out of how many, sample or not, uncertainty, percent or points, who is missing, correlation or causation, smell test. The table maps each question to **what it catches**.
notes.88: Behind each row is a person. The table pairs a field with the experience it records, such as a death recounted to a stranger with a tablet. The obligation holds at row 40,000 as at row 1. A record of disclosed violence with a name and village needs **stricter handling** than the rest of the dataset.
notes.89: Consent is the floor. People need to know what is collected, how it is used and stored, and that they can refuse, in a language they understand. Row two is where our sector fails: when the interviewer also decides eligibility, refusal carries a cost. Test yourself: **if nobody declined last round, you collected signatures**.
notes.90: Removing names is only the beginning. Village plus age plus caste plus occupation can re-identify a person in a small population. Use the four steps in order: remove direct identifiers, coarsen quasi-identifiers, suppress small cells, restrict access. 'It is anonymised' describes **an intention and falls short of a property**.
notes.91: The DPDP Act, 2023 applies to anyone handling personal digital data, NGOs and researchers included, with duties applying from 13 May 2027. Record why each field is collected, be able to act on access, correction and erasure requests, and know who you would tell after a breach. **Being small is no exemption.** Take advice on specifics.
notes.92: An overall average can hide large gaps between groups. A programme can report good totals while failing Dalit, Adivasi, disabled or women beneficiaries. Disaggregation is how inequity becomes visible. The chart is illustrative, so use it to practise asking **which group sits under the average**.
notes.93: Missing data is rarely random. Homeless people, seasonal migrants, people with disabilities, transgender people and unpaid carers are under-counted for the reasons in the table. What is not counted is not funded, so under-counting is a political outcome. **Name the missing in your reports** in one honest sentence.
notes.94: Data power asks who holds the dataset and who supplied it. Communities supply time, answers and risk, and rarely receive a copy of the findings. Two cheap corrections are a budgeted return visit to share results in the local language and a copy of what was collected. Both change **the relationship for the next survey**.
notes.96: Tools matter less than habits. Start with spreadsheets and pivot tables, move to R or Python when the analysis will be repeated or must be reproducible, use Stata or SPSS where collaborators do, and QGIS for anything spatial. **A reproducible spreadsheet beats an undocumented script.** The reason to move on is repeatability.
notes.97: Know where to find free data: data.gov.in, the Census, NFHS, MoSPI and the UDISE+ and HMIS portals. Read the **methodology note before the data**, since it holds the sample design, definitions and lowest valid level. Save each file with its download date because portals revise.
notes.98: Use the reading list for depth. Tufte covers section 5 from the source, Wheelan the concepts in sections 4 and 6, Rosling global statistics, and D'Ignazio and Klein who is counted. Huff is the classic primer and Banerjee and Duflo give development evidence. The NFHS and PLFS notes are free. **An afternoon with the NFHS note** teaches applied data literacy.
notes.99: Close with five reminders: ask where data came from and who is missing, plot before you trust a summary, use the median for money, look for the confounder, handle people's data with care. The table tells you which section to revisit. The habit under all five is to **treat every number as the end of a process with choices in it**.
